title: Data Warehouses: Partitions, Dry Runs, and Paying per Query
intro: Cloud data warehouses separate storage from compute and charge for what a query reads or for how long compute runs. That makes a careless query a billing event. BigQuery charges per byte scanned; Snowflake charges for the time a virtual warehouse is running. The dataset here is analytics, with a table events of several terabytes.

steps.prompt: Before running a query on a big table, ask what it would cost. Dry-run this query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events WHERE user_id = 8812
expected_commands: bq query --dry_run --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events WHERE user_id = 8812'
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events WHERE user_id = 8812'
bq query --dry_run --use_legacy_sql=false "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events WHERE user_id = 8812"
steps.fake_output: Query successfully validated. Assuming the tables are not modified, running this query will process 4120441020440 bytes of data.
steps.hint: bq query --dry_run --use_legacy_sql=false 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events WHERE user_id = 8812'
steps.explanation: 4.1 terabytes would be scanned, to count one user's events.
steps.why: A dry run validates the SQL and reports the bytes it would read, free. At on-demand prices 4 TB is about $25, for one query; in a dashboard that refreshes hourly that's $18,000 a month. The filter on user_id doesn't help: without a matching partition or cluster, a columnar warehouse still reads that whole column for every row.

steps.prompt: See how the table is organised: show its partitioning and clustering settings.
steps.explanation: Partitioned by day on event_date, and clustered by user_id within each partition.
steps.why: A partition is a physically separate slice of the table. A query that filters on the partition column reads only the matching slices; one that doesn't reads them all. Clustering sorts the data inside each partition so that filters on user_id can skip blocks. The table is well designed; the query just didn't use it.

steps.prompt: Dry-run the query again with a partition filter added: AND event_date = '2026-10-01'
expected_commands: bq query --dry_run --use_legacy_sql=false "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events WHERE user_id = 8812 AND event_date = '2026-10-01'"
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events WHERE user_id = 8812 AND event_date = '2026-10-01'"
steps.fake_output: Query successfully validated. Assuming the tables are not modified, running this query will process 9120044 bytes of data.
steps.hint: bq query --dry_run --use_legacy_sql=false "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.events WHERE user_id = 8812 AND event_date = '2026-10-01'"
steps.explanation: 9 megabytes, down from 4.1 terabytes: about 450,000 times less.
steps.why: One extra predicate on the partition column, and the query touches a single day's slice, then clustering narrows it further. This is the most valuable habit in warehouse work: always filter on the partition column. Selecting only the columns you need matters for the same reason, since each column is stored and billed separately; SELECT * on a wide table is the other classic waste.

steps.prompt:
People forget the filter. Which table setting makes the warehouse refuse a query that doesn't have one?
  a) A bigger quota
  b) require_partition_filter: queries without a filter on the partition column are rejected
  c) Deleting old data
  d) A view
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
bq update --require_partition_filter analytics.events

without a filter -> 'Cannot query over table analytics.events without a filter over column(s) event_date'

per query        -> --maximum_bytes_billed=10000000000   (fail instead of scanning more than 10 GB)
steps.hint: Make the expensive mistake impossible, not merely discouraged.
steps.explanation: The table itself can require the filter.
steps.why: A guard rail beats a guideline. With the setting on, the 4 TB query fails with a clear message instead of running. Per-user and per-project quotas on bytes scanned, and a maximum-bytes limit on scheduled queries, cap the damage from everything else. Dashboards and scheduled jobs are where this matters most, because they run unattended and repeatedly (dataeng-incident-002).

steps.prompt: Snowflake charges for the time a virtual warehouse is running, whether queries are executing or not. List the warehouses to see their state and auto-suspend settings.
steps.fake_output:
name          state     size      auto_suspend  auto_resume  running  queued
ANALYTICS_WH  STARTED   LARGE     600           true         0        0
ETL_WH        SUSPENDED X-LARGE   60            true         0        0
ADHOC_WH      STARTED   X-LARGE   NULL          true         0        0
steps.explanation: ADHOC_WH is an extra-large warehouse, running, with no queries and no auto-suspend at all.
steps.why: The opposite pricing model, with the opposite mistake: here an idle warehouse costs the same as a busy one. auto_suspend NULL means it never stops; an X-Large left on is thousands of dollars a month for nothing. Set auto-suspend to a minute or so everywhere, keep auto-resume on, and size warehouses per workload: a bigger one finishes a heavy job sooner for roughly the same cost, and is pure waste for small queries.
